name: Petite Sirah

lines.s10: Petite Sirah is the inky red of California: blueberry, blackberry and black pepper, with a firm grip that calls for rich food.
lines.s20: Petite Sirah is a grape of its own, raised in France as Durif and at home in California. It is nearly black in the glass, with blueberry, blackberry and dark chocolate, full in body and firm in tannin.
lines.s45: Petite Sirah is not a small Syrah, nor Syrah at all. It is a separate grape, a child of Syrah, at home in California, where it long grew among the Zinfandel. It is nearly black in the glass and tastes of blueberry, blackberry and black pepper, with dark chocolate behind. It is full bodied, with a great deal of firm tannin. Most is aged in oak, which adds vanilla and mocha. It wants rich food: braised short rib, barbecue or a burger with blue cheese. A French nurseryman named Durif raised it in the nineteenth century, and Australia still sells it under his name.
lines.sale: Petite Sirah is neither petite nor Syrah: it is an inky red of blueberry, blackberry and black pepper. Have it with the barbecue or a burger with blue cheese, and let me give it some air first.

glass.lead: Blueberry, blackberry and black plum with black pepper and dark chocolate, nearly black, full bodied and thick with firm tannin.

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity medium to medium plus, tannin high, alcohol medium plus to high, body full.

home.home: California, where vines called Petite Sirah have grown since the 1880s, long as a partner of Zinfandel in old mixed vineyards. It is now bottled alone from Napa, Sonoma and Lodi: inky, full and firmly tannic, with blueberry, blackberry and black pepper, usually aged in oak.
home.abroad: France, where it was raised as Durif, has all but given it up. Rutherglen in Australia has grown it since 1908, as Durif, in a dense, ripe style, and Mexico grows it in Baja California.

service.decant: Consider it for a young wine after tasting a sample; air can open the fruit behind the tannin.
service.age: Most within five years; firm, concentrated wines keep ten years and more.

labels.means: The grape's first name, after the French nurseryman who raised it; the name Australia uses.
An old vineyard of several grapes grown and picked together; Petite Sirah is often among them, with Zinfandel.
A warm district of north east Victoria, in Australia, where the grape is sold as Durif.

guest.q: Is Petite Sirah a lighter kind of Syrah?
guest.a: No, and it is not light at all. It is a separate grape, a cross of Syrah and Peloursin, and it is usually darker, fuller and more tannic than Syrah.
The name is thought to come from the berries, which are small. Small berries mean a lot of skin to a little juice, and the skin is where the colour and the tannin come from.
It is the same grape. Durif is its first, French name, after the man who raised it, and Australia still uses it, above all in Rutherglen.

guest.q: Is it really a French grape?
guest.a: By birth, yes: it was raised in a French nursery. France has almost none now, and DNA work at the University of California in the 1990s showed that most of California's old Petite Sirah vines are that same grape.

compare.tell: Syrah, its parent, is more savoury and perfumed, with black olive, smoked meat and violet; Petite Sirah is inkier and more tannic, with little of that savour.
Zinfandel is paler and jammier, with raspberry, a raisin edge and softer tannin; Petite Sirah is nearly black and far more tannic.
Malbec is as dark but plusher, with violet and soft, round tannin; Petite Sirah is firmer and more peppery, with a far heavier grip.

profile.other: Black pepper, liquorice, dark chocolate and black tea; vanilla and mocha from oak; thick, chewy tannin
profile.tell: Inky and staining, with blueberry, black pepper and dark chocolate on a wall of firm tannin: darker and more gripping than Syrah or Zinfandel
profile.regions: California (Napa, Sonoma, Mendocino, Lodi, the Central Valley), Rutherglen in Australia as Durif, Baja California in Mexico
profile.confuse: Syrah is more savoury, with black olive, smoked meat and violet; Zinfandel is paler and jammier, with softer tannin; Malbec is plusher, with violet

cards.front: Petite Sirah: which two grapes are its parents, and its other name?
cards.back: Syrah and Peloursin. It was raised in France in the nineteenth century by a nurseryman named Durif, and Durif is its other name.

cards.front: Where does Australia grow Petite Sirah, and under which name?
cards.back: Rutherglen, in north east Victoria, where it has grown since 1908 and is sold as Durif: dense, ripe and tannic.

cards.front: Petite Sirah blind: what sets it apart from Syrah and Zinfandel?
cards.back: It is inkier and more tannic than either: blueberry, black pepper and dark chocolate on a full, chewy frame. Syrah is more savoury; Zinfandel is paler and jammier.

questions.q: A guest who finds Syrah too heavy sees Petite Sirah on the list and hopes it is a lighter version. What is true of the wine?
opts: It is a separate grape, darker and more tannic
It is Syrah picked early for a lighter style
It is Syrah from young vines
It is a rosé made from Syrah
questions.exp: Petite Sirah is Durif, a cross of Syrah and Peloursin, and it is usually inkier and more tannic than Syrah. The name describes small berries, not a light wine or an early picked Syrah.

questions.q: A blind red is opaque purple and stains the glass, with blueberry, blackberry, black pepper and dark chocolate. It is full bodied, with very firm tannin and no raisin or smoked meat. Which grape is it most likely to be?
questions.exp: Inky colour, blueberry, black pepper and very firm tannin point to Petite Sirah. Zinfandel is paler with a raisin edge, Syrah shows smoked meat and olive, and Cabernet Sauvignon shows cassis and cedar.

questions.q: An Australian list offers a Rutherglen Durif, and a guest asks which grape she would know it as in California. Which is it?
questions.exp: Durif is the first name of Petite Sirah, kept in Australia, where Rutherglen has grown it since 1908. Syrah is one of its parents, not the same grape.

report: Mode home, as the plan fixes it: California is home and France, where the grape was bred, has all but none. Rutherglen Durif is a real second style, and a reviewer could argue for a side by side of California against Australia, but both are New World, so the plan's form is right.
New grape: the profile is written in the manner of GRAPES, and the targets are california, napa-sonoma, rutherglen and mexico, the four pages the Codex's own records tie to the grape or to Durif.
No GRID_SAY: say is puh-TEET sih-RAH with DUR-if, the name used in Australia.

The Codex's records agree: Petite Sirah is Durif, a French cross of Syrah and Peloursin, a partner of Zinfandel in old mixed vineyards, and Rutherglen's dry red as Durif. The Codex dates the cross to a French nursery in the 1880s; pages read through search give about 1880 for the cross and 1868 for the name, so the entry says the nineteenth century and gives no year.

Durif is named, by surname alone, because the grape carries his name; he died in the nineteenth century. The DNA work of the 1990s at the University of California, Davis, which found over nine in ten of the old California vines called Petite Sirah to be Durif, stands on several pages read through search and is given in a guest answer; the rest were other grapes of the old mixed vineyards.

The arrival in California is given as the 1880s; one page gives 1884. The first bottle labelled with the grape's own name is a claim of one winery and is left out. Rutherglen since 1908 stands on the regional body's own history page and two others.
Petite for small berries is the common explanation, hedged as thought to be: one page ties the old name Petite Syrah to a small berried form of Syrah itself.

The ladder: the Court's grid reads Napa and Sonoma as warm for Zinfandel, so Napa stands on the warm rung with Lodi, the Central Valley and Rutherglen, and the moderate rung is Mendocino and the cooler sites of Sonoma. Mendocino and black tea stand on trade profiles, not on a wine body.
No Creole dish is given: the tannin wants beef, smoke and blue cheese.
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open the hosts directly.

checked.verdict: Sound after six fixes in one round. Durif a cross of Peloursin by Syrah, raised in a French nursery about 1880, true Durif in California from 1884, the old California vines proved mostly Durif by DNA at Davis in the late 1990s, and Rutherglen since 1908 were confirmed; the spoken line said neither small beside a guest answer on small berries, three lines said bred where the sources say found and propagated, a guest answer said nearly all where the work found most, and two tells parted the grape from Syrah and Malbec by notes both carry.
changed: lines.s20: Bred says a deliberate cross; the sources say Durif found and propagated a cross of Peloursin by Syrah in his nursery about 1880, and the card and a guest answer already say raised.
lines.s45: Neither small sat beside a guest answer that the name comes from the small berries; not a small Syrah, nor Syrah at all, is the Codex's California record's own wording and keeps both true.
worlds.home.abroad: The same move from bred to raised.
guest.3.a: Nearly all said more than the work found: the vines called Petite Sirah in California proved mostly Durif, with Peloursin and a few others among them.

compare.0.tell: The tell gave Petite Sirah blueberry as a parting note, and the Syrah entry lists blueberry; inkier and more tannic, with little of the savour, parts them as the Codex's California record does.
compare.2.tell: The tell gave Petite Sirah blueberry and dark chocolate as parting notes, and the Malbec entry lists blueberry, cocoa and mocha; a far heavier grip parts them.
open: Mendocino as the moderate rung is not confirmed on a wine body's page.
